newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Police block Anti-APEC protests from summit venue.
newsitem.headline: Police block Anti-APEC protests from summit venue.

text.p: Heavily armed police with riot shields on Sunday blocked a leftist protest convoy from getting onto the main highway leading to the site of this year's APEC summit.

Chanting "Let the people through", foreign delegates to the anti-APEC Peoples Conference on Imperialist Globalisation linked arms and stood in the front ranks of the protest while Roman Catholic nuns behind them prayed with rosary beads.
Most of the thousands of protesters taking part rode in the shiny jeepneys modelled on World War Two jeeps that are the Philippines' most common form of public transport.
"We have the right to pass through," Romeo Capulong, a noted leftist lawyer, told the police blocking the way.
"Our constitution guarantees freedom of assembly and movement," he said.
Many of the locally built jeepneys, which carry 20 people or more, flew streamers with slogans like "Junk APEC" or "Save our natural resources".
The protesters refused to allow police to search the protest vehicles and check drivers' licences.
"It's just a routine check to ensure the security of everybody," Mamerto Agudo, inspector general of the Philippine National Police, told reporters.

The Peoples Conference protest was one of three separate leftist convoys that tried to leave Manila to travel to Subic Bay, some 80 km (50 miles) to the north where U.S. President Bill Clinton and other Asia-Pacific leaders meet on Monday.
A second motorcade was briefly blocked by a police SWAT team wearing black uniforms but was later allowed to proceed.
Eventually it got stuck in the huge traffic jam caused by the police blockade of the first convoy.
Both the Peoples Conference and the Slam APEC convoys had more than 200 vehicles taking part.
The third group, consisting of just 18 jeepneys with both foreign and Filipino protesters, was organised by the Manila People's Forum.
It was travelling under police escort to the northern part of Manila.
Police said they had been told to use "maximum tolerance" in dealing with the protesters but were determined to prevent them reaching the heavily guarded summit venue on a former U.S. naval base.
Security officials are determined to prevent any embarrassment to the government while it plays host to the fourth annual meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.

Philippine intelligence agencies have reported that leftists are planning to launch attacks against the some 6,000 leaders, cabinet ministers and officials attending the summit and the meetings that preceded it.

APEC's 18 members are Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
The three convoys reflect the disarray in the ranks of the Philippine left.

Once the spearhead of a vicious insurgency in the 1970s against President Ferdinand Marcos, the left has been weakened since the overthrow of Marcos by democratic reforms, growing prosperity and internecine feuding.
